facts.fact: Myloplus aylan was described as a new species in 2024 in the journal Neotropical Ichthyology.
The species authors are Pereira, Ota, Machado, Collins, Ândrade, Garcia-Ayala, Jégu, Farias and Hrbek.
It was described in a revision of the black-barred disk pacus, which also redescribed Myloplus schomburgkii and described a second new species, M. sauron.
It belongs to the genus Myloplus in the family Serrasalmidae, the same family as the pacus and piranhas.
For years it was lumped together with Myloplus schomburgkii, the Black Bar Silver Dollar.
The name honours Aylan Moraes Andrade, son of co-author Marcelo Andrade and Carine Moraes, who was born on 23 December 2022 and died on 6 July 2023.
The name is a noun in apposition.
It has a vertical black bar on the flank, usually running from the dorsal-fin base to the tip of the pelvic fin; among its congeners only M. schomburgkii and M. sauron share this bar.
It differs from M. schomburgkii and M. sauron by a parietal bone that is markedly concave in side view and by 82–95 perforated lateral-line scales.
Other diagnostic counts are 40–41 vertebrae, 30–39 prepelvic spines and 21–25 branched dorsal-fin rays.
The three black-barred lineages differ by 7.9–11% in molecular divergence and do not form a natural group.
The video gives the genetic divergence from M. schomburgkii as about 8%.
In life the body is greyish-silver, with orange-red pigment on the head and chest region; the dorsal and caudal fins are yellow at the base and dark at the tips.
The trade fish stand out for their very broad black band across the body.
It was assessed as Least Concern under IUCN criteria because of its wide range in western Amazonia.
The holotype measures 213 mm SL, and the largest paratypes reach about 309 mm SL.
It occurs in the western Amazon basin of Peru and Brazil.
It is recorded from the Nanay, Tigre (a Marañón tributary), Branco, Juruá, Jutaí, Purus, Madeira and Uatumã basins.
The type locality is Lago do Bento on the rio Baraúna, in Caracaraí municipality, Roraima, Brazil.
It lives alongside M. schomburgkii in the rio Água Boa do Univini, a tributary of the rio Branco.
It is most abundant in black-water rivers such as the Nanay in Peru and the Pitinga and Jutaí in Brazil.
In white-water rivers such as the Juruá and Madeira, it was found only in black-water lakes.
It also occurs in clear-water tributaries of the rio Branco, such as the Água Boa do Univini and the Baraúna.
The authors suggest that white-water rivers of Andean origin act as a chemical barrier to its dispersal.
It is caught in small numbers for the ornamental trade, mainly in Peru.
Peru has banned its extraction and sale since 2009 unless the fish come from approved management programmes.
Threats to wild populations include commercial fishing on the upper Solimões, pollution (mainly from mining on the rio Branco) and planned hydroelectric dams on the upper Solimões.
A German importer received it from Colombia as Myloplus schomburgkii 'Big Black Stripe'; the fish were 9–12 cm subadults.
It has probably been in the aquarium trade for years under the name M. schomburgkii.
It grows to over 30 cm, so it is not suitable for small aquariums.
Most published care advice was written when the fish was still identified as M. schomburgkii, so very specific care figures should be treated with caution.
It needs a very large aquarium; a 55-gallon tank is far too small.
The video suggests starting at about 75°F (24°C) in soft water with a pH of about 6 to 7.
Stable water, strong filtration, plenty of oxygen and regular water changes matter more than exact figures.
It produces a lot of waste, so it needs strong filtration.
It is mostly herbivorous and will eat aquarium plants.
Plant foods such as spirulina foods, algae flakes and vegetables should make up much of the diet, with some protein added.
It is active and social and should be kept in groups.
Mature males have a two-lobed anal fin, with the second lobe centred on the 13th or 14th branched ray; females and juveniles have a single broad lobe.
Breeding males are dark over the body, are dark red along the mid-flank, and have dorsal-fin filaments and stiff hooks on the anal-fin rays.
Breeding females have a dark-red to black anal fin and red colouring on the mid-flank around the bar.
Adult males develop elongated dorsal-fin rays, and both sexes can take on red colouring.
Attempts to breed it in captivity have not succeeded.
